subject: geography
prompt: Tap the **submerged, shallow edge of a continent** that is rich in marine life and in resources such as oil and natural gas.

image.alt: A cross-section of the ocean floor from a continent across the deep ocean

hint: It begins right at the coastline and the water above it is shallow.
explanation: The **continental shelf** is the submerged, shallow edge of a continent that extends under the sea. It is rich in **marine life** and in resources like **oil and gas**. Coastal (neritic) fish live over the shelf at depths of about 0–200 m. The steep **continental slope** beyond it marks the true edge of the continent.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the **deepest part** of the ocean floor in this cross-section.

image.alt: A cross-section of the ocean floor from a continent across the deep ocean

hint: Look for a long, narrow gash that plunges below everything else.
explanation: **Ocean trenches** are the deepest parts of the ocean. The **Mariana Trench** in the Pacific Ocean is the deepest place on Earth. The **abyssal plain** is deep, vast and flat, but trenches plunge far below it.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the **immense underwater mountain range formed by volcanic activity**, which is also the longest mountain range in the world.

image.alt: A cross-section of the ocean floor from a continent across the deep ocean

hint: Look for a mountain with a valley split down its middle and magma rising beneath it.
explanation: The **Mid-Ocean Ridge** is an immense underwater mountain range formed by volcanic activity, and it is the world's **longest mountain range**, hidden beneath the ocean. A **rift valley** runs along its crest, with **magma** rising beneath it. A **seamount** is a single underwater mountain, not a long range.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the **guyot**, a flat-topped underwater mountain.

image.alt: A cross-section of the ocean floor from a continent across the deep ocean

hint: Its summit was worn flat by waves before it sank back under the sea.
explanation: A **guyot** is a flat-topped underwater mountain. It is usually a former **seamount** whose summit was worn flat by wave action over thousands of years and which later sank below the sea. The pointed peak beside it is a seamount, and the peak sticking out of the water is a **volcanic island**.

subject: geography
prompt: A submarine travels along the sea floor **from the coast towards the deep ocean**. Arrange the features in the order it meets them.

image.alt: A cross-section of the ocean floor from a continent across the deep ocean

hint: First the shallow ledge, then the steep 'true edge' of the continent.
explanation: The shallow **continental shelf** comes first. At its outer edge the steep **continental slope** marks the true edge of the continent. At the foot of the slope lies the gentler **continental rise**, which leads down to the vast, flat **abyssal plain**.

subject: geography
prompt: Which picture shows a **seamount**?

image.alt: A cross-section of the ocean floor from a continent across the deep ocean

options.text: Picture Q

image.alt: Picture Q: an underwater landform

options.text: Picture P

image.alt: Picture P: an underwater landform

options.text: Picture R

image.alt: Picture R: an underwater landform

hint: A seamount rises from the ocean floor but stays fully under water.
explanation: A **seamount** is an underwater mountain, usually of volcanic origin, that rises from the ocean floor but **does not reach the sea surface** (Picture P). Picture Q has a flat top, so it is a **guyot**, a seamount whose summit was eroded. Picture R breaks the surface, so it is a **volcanic island**. Some underwater mountains, such as **Mauna Kea** (Hawai‘i), are even taller than Mount Everest.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each feature of the ocean floor with its description.

image.alt: A cross-section of the ocean floor from a continent across the deep ocean

right.text: Underwater mountain, usually volcanic, that does not reach the surface
Steep slope that marks the true edge of a continent
Immense underwater mountain range formed by volcanic activity
Vast, flat and deep ocean floor

hint: 'Abyssal' means very deep; 'ridge' means a long chain of mountains.
explanation: The **continental slope** is the steep drop that marks the continent's true edge. The **abyssal plain** is the vast, flat, deep floor. The **mid-ocean ridge** is a long volcanic mountain range, and a **seamount** is a single underwater mountain that does not reach the surface. Together these landforms are called **submarine relief** (or ocean relief), and they affect marine life, resources and undersea exploration.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap a **trough** of this wave.

image.alt: A side view of an ocean wave with two arrows and points A and B

hint: Troughs are the low 'valleys' between the peaks.
explanation: When the sea surface rises and falls alternately, it forms a **wave**. The high peaks are **crests** and the low valleys between them are **troughs**. The dashed line shows the **calm sea level**, and waves are mainly caused by **winds** blowing across the water.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the measurement that shows the **wavelength**.

image.alt: A side view of an ocean wave with two arrows and points A and B

hint: Wavelength is a horizontal distance.
explanation: **Wavelength** is the horizontal distance between two consecutive crests (or two consecutive troughs), so it is the red arrow from crest to crest. The green arrow is vertical, from trough level up to crest level, so it shows the **wave height**. Waves carry energy across the oceans over long distances.

subject: geography
prompt: A buoy floats at point A. In **one minute**, 12 wave crests pass it. What is the **wave frequency**?

image.alt: A side view of an ocean wave with two arrows and points A and B

options.text: 12 crests per second
5 crests per second
0.2 crests per second
720 crests per second

hint: Wave frequency counts crests passing a point each second, not each minute.
explanation: Wave frequency = number of crests passing point A **each second**: $$\dfrac{12\ \text{crests}}{60\ \text{s}} = 0.2\ \text{crests per second}$$ Saying 12 forgets to change minutes into seconds, and 720 multiplies by 60 instead of dividing. 5 comes from $60 \div 12$; that is actually the **wave period** (5 s), the time a crest takes to travel from A to B.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each term with its meaning.

image.alt: A side view of an ocean wave with two arrows and points A and B

right.text: Number of wave crests passing a point each second
Erosion of rock and soil by the force of moving water
Horizontal distance between two consecutive crests or troughs
Time taken by the crest at A to reach B

hint: Period is a time, frequency is a count per second, wavelength is a distance.
explanation: **Wavelength** is a distance (crest to crest). **Wave period** is a time: how long the crest at A takes to reach B. **Wave frequency** is how many crests pass a point every second. **Hydraulic action** is erosion by the force of moving water, which loosens and removes material. It is one way waves shape the coast.

subject: geography
prompt: Waves attack a rocky headland for thousands of years. Arrange the landforms in the order they form.

image.alt: A rocky coast with several rock features carved by the sea

hint: The rock is first opened up, then hollowed out, then broken through, then collapses.
explanation: **Hydraulic action** opens a **crack**. Hydraulic action and abrasion widen it into a **sea cave**. When the back of the cave is eroded through, a **sea arch** forms. The top of the arch collapses under gravity, leaving a tall **sea stack**, which is worn down over time into a **stump**. This is why waves are called **coastal architects**. They also deposit material to build **beaches**.

subject: geography
prompt: An **undersea earthquake** sets off the giant wave in this picture. When it reaches land, what is the height marked **?** called, and how high can it be?

image.alt: A cross-section of the sea with a jolt on the sea floor and a wave heading towards a coast

options.text: Wave height; never more than 3 m
Tidal range; about 12 m
Wavelength; up to 30 m
Run-up height; up to about 30 m, or even more in extreme cases

hint: It is the highest level the water climbs to on land, measured above sea level.
explanation: Giant waves caused mainly by **underwater earthquakes** are called **tsunamis**. On reaching the shore, the greatest vertical height the water reaches above sea level is the **run-up height**, which can be **30 m** or more in extreme cases. Wavelength is a horizontal distance, and tidal range is about tides, not tsunamis.

subject: geography
prompt: The diagram shows four possible positions of the Moon. Tap where the Moon is on a **new moon** day, when a spring tide occurs.

image.alt: The Sun, the Earth with its oceans, and four possible positions of the Moon on its orbit

spots.label: New moon (Moon between Sun and Earth)

hint: On a new moon day, the Moon's lit side faces completely away from us.
explanation: **Spring tides** happen when the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a **straight line**. On a **new moon** day the Moon lies between the Sun and the Earth, and on a **full moon** day it lies on the far side of the Earth. Either way, the Sun and Moon pull together, so high tides are unusually high and low tides unusually low. The top and bottom positions are the **quarter moons**, which give neap tides.

subject: geography
prompt: This chart shows the highest and lowest water level each day for two weeks, **starting on a new moon day**. Tap the day when the Moon is most likely at its **first quarter**.

image.alt: A bar chart of the highest and lowest water level on each day for fifteen days

hint: At the quarter phases the Sun and Moon pull in different directions.
explanation: At the **first- and third-quarter** phases, the Sun and Moon pull in different directions, so the gap between high and low tide is smallest. These are **neap tides**, the shortest bar (around day 7). Days 0 and 14 have the tallest bars, which are **spring tides** at new moon and full moon.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.

image.alt: The Sun, the Earth with its oceans, and four possible positions of the Moon on its orbit

assertion: Spring tides occur on full moon and new moon days.
reason: During neap tides, the difference between high tide and low tide becomes smaller.
hint: Both statements are facts, but does the reason talk about spring tides at all?
explanation: Both are true. Spring tides occur on **full and new moon** days because the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a straight line, so their pull **combines**. The reason is a true fact about **neap tides**, but it does not explain why spring tides happen on those days. So the answer is (b).

subject: geography
prompt: A giant oil tanker needs at least $21\ \text{m}$ of water to pass safely. The channel is $18\ \text{m}$ deep at **low tide** and the **tidal range** is $5\ \text{m}$. How deep is it at high tide, and when can the tanker pass?

image.alt: A cross-section of a shallow sea channel with a giant oil tanker, the low-tide level and the high-tide level

options.text: $23\ \text{m}$; only around high tide
$13\ \text{m}$; it can never pass
$23\ \text{m}$; at any time of day
$18\ \text{m}$; at any time of day

hint: The tidal range is how much higher high tide is than low tide.
explanation: Depth at high tide = low-tide depth + tidal range $= 18 + 5 = 23\ \text{m}$, which is more than the $21\ \text{m}$ needed. At low tide only $18\ \text{m}$ is left, so the ship would **run aground**. It must wait for high tide, just as very large crude carriers do in the shallow **Singapore Strait**. $13\ \text{m}$ comes from subtracting the range, and 'any time' ignores the low tide. This is why ships check **both the water depth and the tidal range** before berthing.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.

image.alt: A cross-section of a shallow sea channel with a giant oil tanker, the low-tide level and the high-tide level

assertion: Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) passing through the Singapore Strait often wait for hours to cross only during high tide.
reason: High tide raises the water level, giving enough depth over shallow areas so the ships do not run aground.
hint: Why would a huge, deep ship care about the water level?
explanation: Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion. The Singapore Strait has **shallow areas**, and high tide gives **sufficient water depth** for these deep tankers. High tides also help ships enter **harbours** more easily. Tidal ranges at some ports reach 4–5 m, and the **Gulf of Khambhat** has one of the highest, about 12 m.

subject: geography
prompt: Tidal currents in a coastal channel flow at $5$ **knots**. If $1$ knot $= 1$ nautical mile per hour and $1$ nautical mile $= 1{,}852\ \text{m}$, what is this speed in km/h?

image.alt: A narrow sea channel with a strong current and a speed dial

options.text: $8.0\ \text{km/h}$
$9.3\ \text{km/h}$
$2.7\ \text{km/h}$

hint: Multiply by the length of a nautical mile, then change metres into kilometres.
explanation: $$5 \times 1{,}852\ \text{m} = 9{,}260\ \text{m per hour} = 9.26 \approx 9.3\ \text{km/h}$$ This fits the chapter's figure that tidal currents can reach **5–6 knots (about 9–11 km/h)**. $9{,}260$ forgets to change metres into kilometres, $2.7$ divides instead of multiplying, and $8.0$ uses an ordinary land mile (about $1.6\ \text{km}$) instead of a nautical mile.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.

image.alt: A sloping beach where the sea creeps up and down, with fish near the shore and a person holding a net

assertion: During high tide, many fish move closer to the shore, so fishing communities can get a better catch.
reason: Tides are caused mainly by winds blowing across the surface of the ocean.

explanation: The assertion is true: at high tide fish come closer to the shore in search of **food and shelter**. The reason is false, because **waves** are mainly caused by winds. **Tides** are caused by the **gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun**. So the answer is (c).

subject: geography
prompt: The picture shows a rocky hillock in the sea, joined to the shore by a stone path. At the **Bhadkeshwar Mahadev Temple** in Dwarka, which stands on such a hillock, when can visitors walk to it?

image.alt: A small rocky hill in the sea joined to the shore by a stone path, with the water level changing

Only during high tide, when the water is deepest
Only on spring-tide days, when high tides are highest
At any time, because the path is never under water

hint: The path is completely submerged at one stage of the tide.
explanation: The temple stands on a small hillock in the **Arabian Sea**. Its stone path is completely **submerged at high tide** (flood tide) and uncovered at **low tide** (ebb tide), so visitors can reach it only at low tide. Tides rise and fall about **twice a day** in most parts of the world.

subject: geography
prompt: The rise and fall of tides can turn turbines like the one shown. Which group lists sites in India named as **major tidal energy sites**?

image.alt: A wall across a bay with a tunnel and a spinning turbine connected to a light bulb

options.text: The Mariana Trench, the Mid-Ocean Ridge and Mauna Kea
The Thar Desert, the Deccan Plateau and the Chota Nagpur Plateau
The Gulf of Mexico, the Labrador coast and Norway
The Gulf of Kutch, the Gulf of Khambhat and the Sundarbans

hint: Tidal energy needs coastal places with a big rise and fall of water.
explanation: The **Gulf of Kutch**, the **Gulf of Khambhat** and the **Sundarbans** are among India's major tidal energy sites. The Gulf of Khambhat has a tidal range of about 12 m. India has a coastline of **11,098.81 km**, but tidal energy is not yet used on a large scale. Inland deserts and plateaus have no tides, and the other options are ocean-floor features or places outside India.

subject: geography
prompt: Select **all** the factors that cause ocean currents.

image.alt: A schematic ocean basin between two land masses with loops of warm and cold currents

options.text: Winds
The Earth's rotation (Coriolis force)
Underwater earthquakes
Differences in temperature and salinity
The shape of continents and ocean basins
The brightness of the full moon

hint: Four factors: one from the air, one from the spinning Earth, one from the water itself, one from the land.
explanation: **Ocean currents** are continuous streams of water flowing in definite directions. They are caused by **winds**, the **Earth's rotation** (Coriolis force), differences in **temperature and salinity**, and the **shape of continents and ocean basins**. Currents flowing from warmer regions are **warm currents** (shown in red) and those from colder regions are **cold currents** (shown in blue). Underwater earthquakes cause tsunamis, not currents.

subject: geography
prompt: Water starts moving **north** in the Northern Hemisphere and **south** in the Southern Hemisphere (dotted lines show straight paths). Which globe shows the paths bent correctly by the **Coriolis force**?

image.alt: A schematic ocean basin between two land masses with loops of warm and cold currents

options.text: Globe Q

image.alt: Globe Q with two arrows starting near the equator

options.text: Globe R

image.alt: Globe R with two arrows starting near the equator

options.text: Globe P

image.alt: Globe P with two arrows starting near the equator

hint: Imagine walking along each arrow. Should it bend to your right or to your left?
explanation: The **Coriolis force**, caused by the Earth's rotation, deflects a freely moving object to the **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and to the **left in the Southern Hemisphere**. Walking north, your right is east. Walking south, your left is also east. So both arrows bend eastwards, as in Globe P. Globe R bends to the right in both hemispheres, and Globe Q has the directions reversed.

subject: geography
prompt: Both coasts lie at high latitudes. **Coast X** stays free of sea ice, but sea ice and icebergs form off **Coast Y**. Which current is most like the one flowing past Coast Y?

image.alt: Two high-latitude coasts side by side, labelled Coast X and Coast Y

options.text: The Gulf Stream, a warm current
A tidal current caused by the Moon's pull
A wind wave set up by a passing storm
The Labrador Current, a cold current

hint: Which current carries freezing water down the east coast of Canada?
explanation: The **Labrador Current** is a **cold current** flowing along the east coast of Canada. It carries freezing water that helps sea ice and icebergs form even at lower latitudes. Coast X is like Norway, which the **warm Gulf Stream** keeps fairly free of ice. Tidal currents and wind waves are not warm or cold currents.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.

explanation: Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion. The warm **Gulf Stream** starts in the Gulf of Mexico in the Atlantic and carries warmth towards **Norway**, so sea ice does not form easily there. This shows that ocean currents **affect the temperature of nearby coasts**.

subject: geography
prompt: Where in this picture would you expect a **rich fishing ground**, and why?

image.alt: A top view of the sea where two different currents meet, with fishing boats

options.text: Where the warm and cold currents meet, because the water there is rich in nutrients
Over the deepest trench, where no sunlight reaches
Where a single warm current flows alone, far from any cold water
Only on the high seas, because coastal waters have no fish

hint: Look at where the tiny green dots and the fish gather.
explanation: Regions where **warm and cold currents meet** are rich in **nutrients**. These nutrients support a large variety of fish, which makes such places important **fishing grounds**. The chapter links rich fishing grounds to the meeting of warm and cold currents, not to trenches, a lone current or the high seas alone.

subject: geography
prompt: Cyclones like this one form over **warm ocean waters**. How are cyclones in the North Indian Ocean given names such as Biparjoy (2023) and Remal (2024)?

image.alt: A huge spinning storm cloud seen from above over a warm sea

By a public vote held after the storm ends
In sequence from a list of 169 names submitted by 13 member countries, including India
From a list of 13 names, one sent by each of 169 countries

hint: The names are picked in turn from a ready-made list shared by several countries.
explanation: Cyclones are large rotating storms caused by **atmospheric disturbances over warm ocean waters**. In the North Indian Ocean they are named **in sequence from a list of 169 names** submitted by **13 member countries**, including India. Names make communication clear and raise public awareness. Option d swaps the two numbers.

subject: geography
prompt: Most deaths in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami occurred in Indonesia, yet the island of **Simeulue** was largely spared. What do researchers suggest helped?

image.alt: An elder telling a story to children on a beach while the sea draws back

options.text: A tall sea wall had been built around the island just before 2004
Local folklore, passed down for generations, helped people recognise the warning signs and act quickly
The island lies far away from the Indian Ocean
Everyone had already been moved to cyclone shelters

hint: Think of stories elders tell, like the one in the picture.
explanation: Researchers suggest that **local folklore** passed down through generations helped Simeulue's residents **recognise a tsunami's warning signs** and respond quickly. This shows how **traditional knowledge** can work alongside modern early warning systems. Public awareness matters as much as technology.

subject: geography
prompt: Which statement about the **2004 Indian Ocean tsunami** is correct?

image.alt: A cross-section of the sea with a jolt on the sea floor and a wave heading towards a coast

options.text: It was caused by a cyclone over the Bay of Bengal
It claimed around 23,000 lives across the region
In India, the damage was limited to the coast of Gujarat
It struck on 26 December 2004, claimed around 2,30,000 lives and led to stronger tsunami early warning systems

hint: Tsunamis come from the sea floor, not the sky, and the toll was in lakhs.
explanation: On **26 December 2004**, the Indian Ocean tsunami claimed around **2,30,000 lives**. In India, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Andhra Pradesh, Keralam and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands suffered extensive damage. The disaster led many countries to set up **tsunami early warning systems**, and India built a real-time network of **tsunami detection buoys** under the ITEWC. Option b drops a zero, and a tsunami is caused by an undersea earthquake, not a cyclone.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each stage of the **tsunami early warning system** with the equipment used.

image.alt: A coast and sea fitted with instruments: a satellite, a buoy, a sensor on the sea floor, a tide gauge, a seismic station and a warning centre

right.text: Ocean Bottom Pressure Recorders (OBPRs) on the seafloor
Satellite links, SMS and other communication channels
A network of seismic stations sensing undersea earthquakes
Coastal tide gauges and radars watching sea level

hint: First sense the earthquake, then watch the sea level, then check on the seafloor, then tell everyone.
explanation: **Detection**: seismic stations pick up undersea earthquakes in real time. **Tracking**: coastal tide gauges and radars follow changes in sea level as the waves arrive. **Confirmation**: OBPRs on the seafloor sense the tsunami passing. **Dissemination**: alerts go by satellite to government agencies and by SMS and other channels to officials and the public.

subject: geography
prompt: Put the steps of a tsunami alert in the correct order.

image.alt: A coast and sea fitted with instruments: a satellite, a buoy, a sensor on the sea floor, a tide gauge, a seismic station and a warning centre

items.text: The Government of India receives the alert
State governments and emergency response teams are informed
The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) issues an alert

hint: The ITEWC reports to the national government, which then passes the message down.
explanation: The earthquake is sensed by **seismic stations**. The **ITEWC** then sends alerts to the **Government of India**, which informs **state governments and emergency response teams**. Satellite networks, SMS, emails and coastal display boards keep the message flowing. Training people to understand warnings is just as important.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each programme or system with what it does.

image.alt: A low coast with sea water pushed inland under a storm, and a raised shelter on higher ground

right.text: Gives financial support for GEMINI devices for fishers
Builds cyclone shelters, strengthens warnings and runs a Decision Support System
Sends tsunami alerts to the Government of India and runs a buoy network
Forecasts cyclone-driven storm surges and how far the coast will flood

hint: 'Matsya' means fish, and a 'storm surge' is sea water pushed inland by a cyclone.
explanation: The **NCRMP** builds cyclone shelters, strengthens warnings, improves emergency response and gives disaster authorities a **Decision Support System**. **SSEWS**, set up by **INCOIS with the IMD**, forecasts storm surges and coastal inundation. The **ITEWC** sends tsunami alerts and runs the buoy network. **PMMSY** gives financial support for **GEMINI** devices.

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange the steps by which a fisher at sea gets a warning through **GEMINI**.

image.alt: A satellite above the sea, a fishing boat with a small device and a phone, and two range lines drawn from the coast

items.text: The INCOIS app decodes it and shows it in a regional language
The GEMINI device on the boat receives the data
The GAGAN satellite sends the information
The device passes the data to the mobile phone by Bluetooth

hint: Start in space and end on the phone screen.
explanation: **GEMINI** (GAGAN-Enabled Mariner's Instrument for Navigation and Information) receives data from the **GAGAN satellite** and sends it to the phone by **Bluetooth**. The **INCOIS app** then shows it in one of **nine regional languages**. Fishers get alerts about high waves, strong winds, cyclones and tsunamis, plus potential fishing zones, current speeds and **bathymetry** data (maps of underwater depth and landforms).

subject: geography
prompt: Today GEMINI's channel reaches up to **50 nautical miles** into the sea. The upgraded two-way system is meant for fishers who travel up to **300 nautical miles**. How many times farther is that?

image.alt: A satellite above the sea, a fishing boat with a small device and a phone, and two range lines drawn from the coast

options.text: 250 times
6 times
350 times
about 0.17 times

hint: 'How many times' means divide the bigger distance by the smaller one.
explanation: $$\dfrac{300\ \text{NM}}{50\ \text{NM}} = 6$$ The new reach is **6 times** farther. 250 is the *difference* $(300 - 50)$, 350 is the sum, and 0.17 is the ratio upside down $(50 \div 300)$. The upgrade will also let fishers **send feedback** (two-way communication), at first as a pilot.

subject: geography
prompt: Select **all** the correct statements about why marine resources matter.

They also have **cultural** value: cowrie shells were once used as currency. They must be used **responsibly**, without harming marine ecosystems.

prompt: Match each numbered object in the picture with the type of marine resource it uses.

Non-living: minerals and materials such as sand and gravel

subject: geography
prompt: Fish group **A** lives over the continental shelf, at depths of about **0–200 m**. What are such fish called?

options.text: Coastal (neritic) fish
Oceanic fish
Submerged aquatic vegetation
Bioactive natural products

Fish, marine bio-organisms, submerged aquatic vegetation and bioactive natural products are all **living** marine resources.

subject: geography
prompt: The three circles show the parts of the **Blue Economy**. Which description matches the World Bank's definition?

Stopping all economic activity at sea
Sustainable use of ocean resources for economic growth, better livelihoods and jobs, while keeping marine ecosystems healthy
Trade carried out only on the high seas

explanation: The World Bank defines the **Blue Economy** as the **sustainable use of ocean resources** to promote **economic growth**, **improved livelihoods and jobs**, while preserving the **health of the marine ecosystem**. Over-exploiting resources (a) harms ecosystem health, and stopping all activity (b) gives up growth and jobs.

subject: geography
prompt: **SDG 14: Life Below Water** has several key aims. Select **all** that are among them.

image.alt: An underwater scene: a healthy coral reef on one side and rubbish and an oversized net on the other

options.text: Reduce marine pollution
Increase subsidies that encourage overfishing
Address ocean acidification
Regulate fishing
Let ships dump waste freely on the high seas
Conserve marine areas

hint: The goal protects life below water. Two options would harm it.
explanation: The UN's **SDG 14** aims to **reduce marine pollution**, **protect marine ecosystems**, **address ocean acidification**, **regulate fishing**, **conserve marine areas**, **eliminate harmful subsidies** and **increase economic benefits** from the sea. It *removes* harmful subsidies rather than adding them, and dumping waste is the opposite of reducing pollution.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the zone where the coastal country has **near-complete control** and can make laws on customs, immigration and pollution, but foreign ships still have the right of **innocent passage**.

image.alt: A top view of the sea beside a coast, divided into bands by distance from the baseline

hint: It is the sea zone closest to the baseline, reaching out to 12 NM.
explanation: The **territorial sea** (territorial waters) reaches **12 nautical miles** from the baseline. Here the country has near-complete control, as it does on land, but foreign ships may pass through under **innocent passage**. Inside the baseline lie **internal waters**. The 12–24 NM band is the **contiguous zone**, where control is only limited.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the part of the sea that belongs to **no single country** and is treated as part of the **global commons**.

image.alt: A top view of the sea beside a coast, divided into bands by distance from the baseline

hint: It lies beyond every country's Exclusive Economic Zone.
explanation: Beyond the **EEZs** (200 NM from the baseline) lie the **high seas**, or international waters. They cover about **64%** of the world's oceans and belong to no single country, so all countries have equal rights there. On the high seas, a ship follows the laws of its **flag state**, the country where it is registered.

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange the maritime zones from the **land outwards**.

image.alt: A top view of the sea beside a coast, divided into bands by distance from the baseline

hint: Use the distances: inside the baseline, then 12 NM, 24 NM and 200 NM.
explanation: **Internal waters** lie inside the baseline. The **territorial sea** reaches 12 NM, the **contiguous zone** 24 NM and the **Exclusive Economic Zone** 200 NM, all measured from the baseline. Beyond that are the **high seas**. International law, especially **UNCLOS**, defines these zones.

subject: geography
prompt: A country's territorial sea reaches **12 nautical miles** from its baseline. If $1$ nautical mile $= 1{,}852\ \text{m}$, about how many **kilometres** is that?

image.alt: A globe with a tiny arc of latitude enlarged into a measured distance at sea

options.text: $6.5\ \text{km}$

hint: Multiply to get metres, then divide by 1,000.
explanation: $$12 \times 1{,}852\ \text{m} = 22{,}224\ \text{m} \approx 22.2\ \text{km}$$ $22{,}224$ km forgets to change metres into kilometres, $6.5$ km divides instead of multiplying, and $19.3$ km uses an ordinary land mile (about $1.6$ km). A **nautical mile** equals one **minute of latitude**, which makes it handy for charts and navigation.

subject: geography
prompt: A fishing boat is **30 nautical miles** from a country's baseline. How much farther must it sail straight out to sea to reach the **high seas**?

image.alt: A top view of the sea beside a coast, divided into bands by distance from the baseline

options.text: 230 NM
170 NM
176 NM
188 NM

hint: The high seas begin where the EEZ ends. How far from the baseline is that?
explanation: The EEZ ends **200 NM from the baseline**, so the boat needs $$200 - 30 = 170\ \text{NM}$$ (it is now inside the EEZ). 230 adds instead of subtracting. 176 and 188 subtract the 24 NM or 12 NM zone limits instead of the boat's own distance of 30 NM. Every limit is measured **from the baseline**.

subject: geography
prompt: Customs officers stop a **smuggling boat 20 nautical miles** from the baseline. In which zone is the boat, and what power does the country have there?

image.alt: A top view of the sea beside a coast, divided into bands by distance from the baseline

options.text: Contiguous zone: limited control over customs, fiscal matters and illegal immigration
Territorial sea: near-complete control, as on land
High seas: only the boat's flag state can act
Internal waters: full control with no right of passage

hint: 20 NM lies between the 12 NM and 24 NM lines.
explanation: The **contiguous zone** stretches from the baseline up to **24 NM**, beyond the 12 NM territorial sea. Here the country has **limited control** over **customs, fiscal matters and illegal immigration**, enough to act against smugglers. At 20 NM the boat is outside the territorial sea and far from the high seas.

subject: geography
prompt: Ships P, Q and R are foreign ships in a country's territorial sea. Which one is making **innocent passage**?

image.alt: A top view of the sea near a coast with three ships labelled P, Q and R

options.text: Ship Q, which has stopped to fish
Ship R, which has dropped anchor though it has no emergency
Ship P, which is sailing straight through without stopping
Ships P and Q, because fishing is a peaceful activity

hint: Innocent passage means moving continuously, and it does not include fishing.
explanation: **Innocent passage** lets foreign ships cross a country's territorial waters as long as they do not threaten its **peace, good order or security**. They must keep moving **continuously**, stopping only for emergencies or breakdowns. It does **not** allow fishing, military operations or other non-peaceful activities. So only Ship P qualifies.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.

image.alt: A top view of the sea beside a coast, divided into bands by distance from the baseline

assertion: A coastal country fully owns and controls the waters of its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ).
reason: Under UNCLOS, a coastal country has special rights to use resources such as fish, oil and gas in its EEZ.
hint: Can ships of other countries still pass peacefully through an EEZ?
explanation: The assertion is false: the country **does not fully own or control** the waters of its EEZ, and other countries' ships may still pass peacefully. The reason is true: **UNCLOS** gives the coastal country **special rights to use resources** such as fish, oil and gas up to **200 NM** from the baseline. So the answer is (d).

subject: geography
prompt: Select **all** the rights that every country enjoys on the **high seas**.

image.alt: Far out at sea: ships flying different flags, a plane, a fishing boat, a cable on the seabed and a survey vessel

options.text: Navigation
Laying undersea cables
Claiming the area as one country's own territory
Fishing
Exploring for minerals
Applying the laws of the nearest coastal country to every passing ship

hint: The high seas are global commons: shared by all and owned by none.
explanation: On the **high seas** all countries have equal rights to **navigate**, **fish**, **fly over**, **lay undersea cables**, build lawful structures such as artificial lands, and **explore for minerals**. No country can claim them. Ships follow the laws of their **flag state**, not the nearest coast. Because no one controls them, problems like **overfishing**, illegal fishing and resource conflicts arise.

subject: geography
prompt: These two ships are on crossing paths. Which set of rules tells them who must **give way**, which side to pass on, how fast to go and which **lights and sound signals** to use?

image.alt: Two ships seen from above on paths that cross, each showing coloured side lights

options.text: MARPOL
COLREGs
UNCLOS
SDG 14

hint: These are the 'rules of the road at sea' for preventing collisions.
explanation: **COLREGs** (Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea) are the 'rules of the road at sea'. They cover keeping a proper lookout, give-way and stand-on vessels, passing sides, safe speed, and lights, sound signals and shapes. **MARPOL** deals with pollution from ships, **UNCLOS** defines maritime zones, and **SDG 14** is the UN goal for life below water. Such rules keep the oceans safe, clean and open for trade.
